content: Food preparation and service areas, as well as the transportation of food to remote locations, must be organized in a manner that ensures a logical flow. This flow should minimize cross-traffic or backtracking and maintain a clear separation between clean and soiled operations. The movement of food through a vessel should follow a systematic sequence, starting from the purveyor at dockside, through storage, preparation, and finishing areas, to the service areas, and finally to the waste management area. This design aims to facilitate smooth and rapid food preparation and service while adhering to strict time and temperature control requirements, minimizing handling and time delays. The Vessel Sanitation Program (VSP) evaluates the size of specific rooms or areas and the flow of food through the vessel during the plan review process. Blast chillers should be incorporated into the design of passenger and crew galleys. Depending on the vessel's size, the intended application of the chillers, and the distances between chillers, storage, and service areas, more than one unit may be required. Blast chillers should also be installed in meat, fish, and vegetable preparation rooms, cold pantries, garde mangers, and other areas where personnel wash or soak food. In vegetable preparation rooms, an automatic vegetable washing machine may be used in addition to food preparation sinks. The main pot washing area, which serves the entire galley operation, should be equipped with at least a three-compartment sink with a prewash station or a four-compartment sink with an insert pan and overhead spray. The sink must be large enough to accommodate the largest piece of equipment, such as pots or tableware, used in its designated serving area. If desired, an automatic warewashing machine with separate prewash stations may be used alongside the three-compartment sinks, provided the machines are appropriately sized for the equipment being washed. A front-loading, pass-through, or conveyor-type warewashing machine is preferable to an under-counter model. Additional three-compartment sinks with prewash stations or four-compartment sinks with insert pans and overhead sprays should be provided in high-use areas, such as bakeries, butcher shops, and other preparation areas where the size of the facility or distance makes the use of a central pot washing area impractical. All food preparation areas should have easy access to a three-compartment sink or a warewashing machine with an adjacent dump sink and prewash hose. Beverage dispensing equipment should be furnished with easily removable drip trays or built-in drains in the tabletop. Bulk milk dispensers and condiment dispensing equipment should also have readily removable drip trays. Storage areas should be designed to accommodate all equipment and utensils used in food preparation areas, such as ladles and cutting blades. The design of installed equipment must ensure that food and wash water drainage is directed into a deck drain, scupper, or deck sink, and not directly or indirectly onto the deck. Utility sinks should be provided in areas such as beverage stations where it is necessary to refill pitchers or dispensers or discard liquids like coffee. Ice cream, sherbet, or similar product dipper wells should be equipped with running water and proper drainage. Ice bins, food display cases, and other food and ice holding units should have tight-fitting doors or protective closures to prevent contamination of stored products. Countertop openings and rims of food cold tops, bains-marie, ice wells, and other drop-in type food and ice holding units should be protected with a raised integral edge or rim of at least 5 mm (3/16 inch) above the counter level around the opening. All surfaces of food contact, splash contact, and exposed non-food contact areas must be smooth, durable, and non-corroding. These surfaces should be easily cleanable and designed without unnecessary edges, projections, or crevices. Only materials approved for food contact should be used on food contact surfaces. Food contact surfaces must be smooth, durable, non-corroding, easily cleanable, readily accessible, and maintainable. Corners should be coved and preferably seamless, in accordance with current sanitary standards for food service equipment. External corners and angles should have a sufficient radius to permit proper drainage and avoid sharp edges. Sealants used on food contact and splash contact surfaces must be approved for food contact (certified to ANSI/NSF Standard 51 or equivalent criteria). Approved sealants should be used sparingly and only when necessary for practical function or design, such as joining surfaces between ice makers and bins. Excessive use of sealant should be avoided. Materials approved for food contact surfaces should also be used for splash contact surfaces. Non-food contact surfaces should be made of durable, non-corroding materials and designed to be smooth, easily cleanable, and accessible.
